articles.title: Xi, Trump and Putin to Meet in Shenzhen
paragraphs: China said on Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in the southern city of Shenzhen on Thursday. If it goes ahead, it will be the first time the three leaders have ever sat down together. The meeting will take place on the edge of the APEC summit, a yearly gathering of leaders from Asia-Pacific economies.

The idea began last month, when the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin had proposed a three-way meeting to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. Moscow and the White House had already announced the meeting before Beijing confirmed it. Mr. Xi has met Mr. Trump three times since October 2025, and he has met Mr. Putin more than 40 times since he became president in 2013.

The agenda is still unclear. China did not say what will be discussed. The White House says Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear weapons around the world and about the war involving the United States, Israel and Iran. It does not expect him to raise Ukraine, although Russia wants that topic to be a priority. Trade is also likely to come up, because a truce between Washington and Beijing will expire in January. Many analysts expect it to be extended.

Experts are cautious about what the summit can achieve. One analyst said the main obstacle is a disagreement over the agenda, and that a joint statement on Ukraine or on sanctions against Russia looks unlikely. Another called the event almost entirely a photo opportunity that raises China's standing. Others noted that simply bringing the two rivals to the table gives Mr. Xi a political benefit, whatever the final result.

articles.title: Taiwan's Foreign Investment Hits a Record High
paragraphs: Taiwan approved a record amount of foreign direct investment in the first ten months of this year. According to the Ministry of Economic Affairs, the total reached US$20.899 billion between January and October, the first time the figure has passed US$20 billion for that period. It covers 1,878 applications and is 127.5 percent higher than a year earlier.

Much of the increase came from one company. The U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology was approved to invest US$9.449 billion in its Taiwanese subsidiary. Other large projects include US$1.248 billion from Denmark's Orsted and US$1.054 billion for a green energy company based in the Netherlands. By source, Singapore was the biggest investor, with 51.71 percent of the total, followed by the United Kingdom with 9.12 percent.

Money is also flowing out of Taiwan at a fast pace. Approved outbound investment totaled US$69.916 billion across 612 applications, more than double last year's level. TSMC, the world's leading contract chipmaker, accounted for a large share, including US$20 billion for its factories in Arizona and US$30 billion for a company that manages its global financial investments. Nanya Technology and GlobalWafers also received approval for overseas spending.

Investment in China moved in the opposite direction. Taiwanese projects approved for China totaled only US$786 million, down 20.04 percent from a year earlier. Chinese investment in Taiwan was even smaller, at US$8.564 million, a fall of more than 91 percent. The figures suggest that Taiwan's chip industry is spreading its operations across more countries, while becoming a more attractive place for foreign companies to build new capacity.

articles.title: Nvidia Leadership Crisis Splits Silicon Valley
paragraphs: Nvidia, the company at the heart of the artificial-intelligence boom, is grappling with an extraordinary leadership vacuum. Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive and board member following reports about his private conduct, including a relationship with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. Colette Kress, the longtime finance chief, is serving as interim chief executive while the board conducts an independent investigation and searches for a permanent successor.

Remarkably, a campaign to bring him back has gathered momentum. An online petition calling for his reinstatement and a fair inquiry has attracted nearly 180,000 signatures, and prominent backers include Elon Musk and several Silicon Valley chief executives. The Financial Times reported that Mr. Huang has discussed a comeback with confidants and that allies are assembling a so-called war room to seek White House support. Two prominent investors have likewise urged the board to weigh every option before making a permanent decision.

Opinion is sharply divided. President Donald Trump said he would not mind Mr. Huang returning, whereas Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that Nvidia must look outside for its next leader, and he questioned whether the company had pursued questionable chip sales to inflate revenue. One analyst dismissed the prospect of a return as a non-starter, pointing out that an ongoing investigation makes a swift reversal far harder than Sam Altman's reinstatement at OpenAI in 2023, which stemmed from a governance dispute. Another suggested that a comeback would be good for the share price, provided the board imposed guardrails.

The stakes extend well beyond one boardroom. American lawmakers are preparing to scrutinize whether the episode has undermined the country's lead in AI and what it means for national security. Taiwan's central bank governor predicted only a short-lived disruption for the island's AI suppliers, which depend heavily on Nvidia's orders. Investors will get their first real glimpse of the interim leadership when the company reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday.
